summary: We developed the Lunar Landing Navigator, a 3D web tool that rates any point at the lunar south pole as a landing site for 2027 and 2028. It uses official NASA maps of sunlight, permanent shadow, Earth visibility and terrain, plus ice detections from the M3 instrument. It also tracks the real positions of the Sun and Earth hour by hour. Four conditions (energy, communication, water and terrain) form a Venn diagram drawn on the pole’s real geography. Pick a point and the system gives a 0–100 suitability score with an explanation, the best landing windows and the communication blackouts. It also simulates how the Sun and shadows move. It includes 26 known sites and found 5 new zones that meet all four conditions. This answers the challenge by turning complex data into clear decisions anyone can follow. It matters because Artemis IV and several robotic missions will land there, where light, contact with Earth and water ice decide whether a mission survives.
details:
What it does and how it works

Intelligent Lunar Landing Software is a 3D web app that rates any point at the lunar south pole as a landing site for 2027 robotic missions and Artemis IV in 2028. Users click the map or type coordinates. They get a 0–100 suitability score, a plain-language explanation and the best landing windows. Four conditions form a Venn diagram drawn on the pole's real geography:

Energy: Sun visible at least 55% of the time.

Communication: Earth visible at least 50% of the time.

Water: within 5 km of a permanently shadowed cold trap.

Terrain: slope of 8° or less.

For each point, the app traces the terrain horizon in 360 directions and computes the Sun and Earth positions hour by hour. That gives the longest night, the longest communication blackout and the best 7–10 day windows. A guided tour builds the Venn layer by layer, then shows the best site.

Benefits

It turns large scientific datasets into decisions anyone can follow.

It covers 26 known sites: NASA's Artemis regions, peaks of light, 2027 missions and past landings.

It found 5 new zones that meet all four conditions.

Users can adjust the criteria and watch the results update instantly.

Intended impact

Support mission planners, students and the public in understanding why landing site choice decides whether a mission survives. It also brings the Artemis program closer to non-experts.

Tools

Languages: Python (NumPy, Pillow, Skyfield) and JavaScript, HTML/CSS and GLSL shaders.

3D and rendering: three.js with WebGL; Web Workers compute the moving shadows.

Testing: headless Chrome with Playwright.

Data:

NASA PGDA/LOLA maps of sunlight, permanent shadow, Earth visibility and terrain.

Ice detections from the M3 instrument (Chandrayaan-1).

JPL DE421 positions of the Sun and Earth, with the IAU model for the Moon's orientation.

AI: Claude helped with development.

Hardware: none needed; it runs in any browser.

Creativity

The Venn diagram follows real ridges and craters, not circles. Users can follow the Sun from a chosen site and watch it circle the horizon while shadows move across the terrain.

Factors considered

Energy, communication, water access, slope, landing ellipse size, mission dates and length, data resolution and uncertainty, and mobile use. We checked the results against the source data:

Horizons agree with 80 m data within 0.1–0.3° on average.

Shadows match the hour-by-hour site analysis in at least 98% of cases.
